name: Sarpapureeswarar Temple, Paamani (Mannargudi)
deity: Shiva as Sarpapureeswarar (Naganathar), with the goddess Amirtha Nayaki
tradition: Shaiva — a Paadal Petra Sthalam, sung in the Tevaram
summary: A short way north of Mannargudi, at the village now called Paamani, stands a Paadal Petra Sthalam where Shiva is worshipped as Sarpapureeswarar, also called Naganathar — the lord of the serpents' city — with the goddess Amirtha Nayaki. Its historical name is Tiruppaadhaleeswaram, and it was praised in a hymn of the child-saint Tirugnana Sambandar. A modest delta shrine with an ancient name, it is a quiet member of the great Tevaram landscape.

sections.history: The temple at Paamani, about three and a half kilometres north of Mannargudi, is an ancient Shaiva site whose historical name is Tiruppaadhaleeswaram. It is counted among the Paadal Petra Sthalams, the shrines praised in the Tevaram, with a hymn attributed to Tirugnana Sambandar. The present stone fabric belongs broadly to the Chola period and later renovation; like many smaller delta temples, its documented history is slight, and its standing rests chiefly on its place in the Tevaram canon.
sections.architecture: The temple follows the Dravidian plan, with a gopuram, a modest prakara and the sanctum of Sarpapureeswarar, the lingam worshipped as Naganathar. The goddess Amirtha Nayaki has her own shrine. As a village temple it keeps the quiet, intimate scale typical of the lesser-known Paadal Petra shrines, without the towering gateways of the great delta centres.
sections.legends: The names Sarpapureeswarar and Naganathar connect the lord to the serpents, nagas, who in the Shaiva tradition are devotees of Shiva and whose worship is associated with relief from the afflictions ascribed to the naga-dosha. Devotees accordingly come here with prayers concerning serpent-related doshas and for general well-being. The detailed sthala-purana of this small shrine is less widely recorded than those of the larger temples nearby.
sections.festivals: The temple keeps the Shaiva festival calendar — Maha Shivaratri, Pradosham and the Margazhi observances — at the quieter scale of a village shrine. Pradosham, especially, draws devotees given the temple's serpent associations, and local observances mark the Tamil months.
sections.experience: Paamani offers the pilgrim the unhurried devotion of a small delta temple with a venerable name. Away from the crowds of the famous centres, the darshan of Sarpapureeswarar is a quiet one, and the temple rewards those who seek out the lesser-known shrines of the Tevaram with the sense of an old sanctity carefully kept.

visit.timings: Typically open from early morning to midday and again from late afternoon into the evening; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected, with shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left at the entrance.
visit.photography: Photography is generally allowed in the outer corridors but not inside the sanctum; ask temple staff before photographing rituals.
visit.gettingThere: Paamani is about 3.5 km north of Mannargudi in Tiruvarur district; Mannargudi is the nearest rail head and town, with local buses and autos to the village.
